title: What Democrats’ Sweeping Midterm Wins Could Mean for the Redistricting Battle
author: Chantelle Lee
body:
Republicans and Democrats in several states engaged in a bitter fight to redraw congressional maps in their parties’ favor leading up to this year’s midterms. But in the aftermath of the blue wave that swept across the country, that conflict may be dying down—at least for now.

Typically, maps are redrawn after the results of the U.S. census are released each decade, in order to account for population and demographic changes. Last year, however, President Donald Trump urged members of his party to redistrict mid-cycle ahead of the 2026 election as the GOP vied to hold onto its narrow House majority. Several Republican-led states moved to do so in the ensuing months, while Democratic leaders in other states responded with their own redistricting efforts, with varying degrees of success.

The sweeping Democratic victories in the midterms, though, could mark a shift in the redistricting battle, political experts tell TIME.

Read More: Are Democrats’ Stunning Midterm Upsets in Deep-Red States a Blip—or Is Their Map Expanding?

Costas Panagopoulos, a professor of political science at Northeastern University, says that Republicans may be more reluctant to push for redistricting mid-cycle going forward, given that their efforts failed to counteract the blue wave in this year’s election.

In states like Texas, North Carolina, Ohio, Alabama, and Florida, Democratic candidates came out on top in multiple districts that had been redrawn to benefit Republicans—which political experts have largely attributed to the fact that, despite redistricting efforts, Republicans were still facing a challenging political climate at a time when Trump’s approval rating was at a historic low.

“In recent years, Democrats have been reluctant to engage in mid-cycle redistricting. Republicans have been more willing to do that, and Democrats have followed suit in response in order to counteract some of the districts created by Republicans to advantage themselves,” Panagopoulos says.

“But as 2026 showed us, those efforts often amount to very little and can even backfire, so I think both parties right now are cautious about any mid-cycle redistricting efforts, and 2026 suggests that even if districts are very heavily gerrymandered to advantage one party or the other, there are no guarantees that those parties will win,” he continues.

Mark Jones, a professor of political science at Rice University, says that, for Republicans, “pretty much anything that they could have done, they already did.” And he says that even if there are states where additional redistricting could in theory help make maps even more favorable for Republicans, GOP lawmakers will now face a challenging time pushing such legislation through if their power in the state governments was reduced—for instance, in Texas, where Democrats gained control of the state House and the governorship.

Meanwhile, the Democrats who were advocating for redistricting in recent months were doing so as “defensive measures,” says Alvin Tillery, the director of Northwestern University’s Center for the Study of Democratic Governance and a Democratic pollster and consultant. And Jones says that, with the party’s sizable victories in this year’s midterms, “the sense of urgency” to redistrict “is no longer there.”

It’s possible, Jones says, that some “unfinished business” may continue—for instance, Virginians passed a redistricting ballot measure in April, but the state Supreme Court prevented the newly drawn maps from taking effect; Jones says that Democrats could try to take up that effort again.

But generally speaking, “I don’t think we’re going to see the gerrymander armed race in 2027 that we saw in 2025,” Jones says. If some of those efforts do proceed, he says, “I think it’s going to be at the margins.”

“The Democratic Party reluctantly engaged in mid-decade redistricting only after Donald Trump and Republicans drew first blood, and given the size of the victory and the lesser the sense of urgency and need to bolster the number of seats that are safely Democratic, I think we’re going to see Democrats try to return to the norms that have governed U.S. politics in the modern era,” Jones says.

That doesn’t mean that partisan gerrymandering has come to an end, experts point out. The next redistricting cycle will take place after the 2030 census, and Panagopoulos says, “When it’s a redistricting cycle, both parties engage to the extent that they can in partisan gerrymandering.” And Democrats, he says, “will remain better positioned to engage in pro-Democratic redistricting in part because of the gains that they made in state legislatures and governorships across the country.”

“I don’t think redistricting is high on any party’s agenda at the moment,” Panagopoulos says. But, he continues, “Things will clearly shift in the aftermath of the 2030 survey, and what will be more important is what the partisan makeup of states and state legislatures looks like at that time.”
